answer: Document the trial as an E16 Measurement, not an E14 Condition Assessment. The observatory's actual procedure -- running the chronometer against its regulator clock for eleven days and noting the accumulated gain/loss at noon -- is exactly E16's scope: a systematic, objective procedure of direct observation yielding a quantifiable value. Model the chronometer as E22 Human-Made Object (P39 measured), the observatory (E39/E74 Actor, P14 carried out by) producing the daily rate as an E54 Dimension (P40 observed dimension; P90 has value / P91 has unit), over the eleven-day E52 Time-Span (P4 has time-span). E14 Condition Assessment is the wrong fit: its necessary property P35 has identified requires an E3 Condition State, and E3's own scope note and examples ('wrecked', 'ruined', 'cockled') are about prevailing physical/material preservation state, not functional performance or accuracy. 'Fit for sea service' is not a preservation judgment -- it is the practical conclusion drawn from the measured rate, not a separate act needing its own class. The certificate itself is an E31 Document that documents (P70, necessary on E31) the E16 Measurement; its 'fit for sea service' wording is the document's informational content, not evidence of a second, condition-assessment activity.

rejected_alternatives.why_not: concept E14 requires (necessary) P35 has identified -> E3 Condition State; concept E3's scope note and examples ('wrecked', 'ruined', 'the topography ... described as cockled') show E3 is about prevailing physical/material preservation state, not timekeeping accuracy or seaworthiness. Nothing in the case describes inspecting wear or damage -- the observatory only ever compares the chronometer's readings to its own regulator clock.
